Three stuck states: a simpler understanding

There are three ways your nervous system can get stuck. Just three. Not thirty. Not three thousand. Three.

The Polyvagal Theory lists many autonomic primary and mixed states: ventral vagal safety, sympathetic flight/fight, dorsal vagal shutdown, plus the mixed states derived from those. Many states, but you don’t get stuck in all of them.

Just three: shutdown, freeze, or flight/fight.

This simplification is extremely useful. Once you narrow down to three, you can narrow down even further and identify which of the three is running things within yourself, quietly driving your every thought, feeling, and action. Then you stop being at the mercy of a vague, shapeless “something’s wrong” and you start working with what’s actually happening in your body.

This page maps all three:

  • Stuck shutdown (numbness, depression, disconnection)
  • Stuck freeze (panic, rage, overwhelm)
  • Stuck fight-or-flight (anxiety, anger)

For each stuck state, you’ll see what it looks like across four observable columns, why your system goes there, and what coming out actually involves.

This page is the third in a three-page series. The first, The Polyvagal Current, introduces the model: three circles for the autonomic states flowing in a continuous current, plus a Safety Influence slider that determines whether each branch shows up regulated or stuck. The second, How to read your own nervous system, teaches the daily literacy practice for using the model on yourself. If either of those is new ground, start there. The series works as a set: the Current is the map of how your nervous system moves; the literacy page teaches you to read it; this page is the map of where it gets stuck.

A reminder if needed: stuck isn’t broken. A stuck nervous system is doing exactly what it evolved to do when the situation it was facing was too much, too long, or too dangerous to move through cleanly. The fact that it’s stuck doesn’t mean something is wrong with you. It means your system did the thing it knew how to do, and now it’s waiting for enough safety to release.

The good news is that “enough safety” is something you can actually work with! And that’s the entire second half of this page.

Quick orientation

Which stuck state am I in?

The short answer: one of three.

Stuck dorsal is shutdown: heavy, numb, cold, retreated. You can’t get out of bed. Nothing matters. The dial is at zero.

Stuck sympathetic is fight-or-flight: racing, urgent, tight, on edge. Heart fast, thoughts narrow, can’t slow down, can’t sleep.

Stuck freeze is the overlap of the two: your heart is pounding but you can’t move; your mind is racing but you can’t think. Activation underneath, brake on top.

To tell which one you’re in right now, read four observable signals: your thoughts, your emotions, your body sensations, and your action impulses. Foggy and heavy points to shutdown. Racing and tight points to fight-or-flight. Activation underneath a blocked impulse points to freeze. The rest of this page walks through each one in detail, plus what coming out of each actually involves.

If you can’t read yourself at all right now, read this companion page: How to read your own nervous system.

The mechanism

What “stuck” means in the Polyvagal Current

In the Polyvagal Current, every state of your nervous system has a regulated expression and a stuck expression. Same state. Different output. Your level of ventral vagal safety activation determines which state is active and your level of stuckness.

With enough safety, the slider sits near the top and you get safety, play, and stillness.

Without enough safety, the slider sits near the bottom and the same three autonomic branches produce the three stuck states this page is about: shutdown, flight/fight, and freeze.

(Ventral itself doesn’t really have a “stuck” version. When safety drops, ventral simply decreases. The newer social engagement system steps back and lets the older defensive autonomic branches take over. The three stuck states are stuck versions of the other two branches, plus the freeze overlap.)

Why “stuck”? Because stuck inherently means there is momentum to move forward, but something is stopping the momentum. Your system is always trying to regulate. There is indeed momentum. But something is blocking regulation.

This reframe matters in practice. The path out of a stuck state isn’t to fight it, fix it, or suppress it. The path out is to ask: what is my system not getting that it needs to be able to move? The answer is more ventral vagal safety in small, repeated, sustainable doses, delivered through specific practices and relationships that meet your specific system.

The rest of this page walks through each stuck state in detail. One might describe your current stuckness, but it’s very possible that you’ll experience some degree of stuckness in the others. I invite you to read through them all.

          State one

          Stuck dorsal vagal shutdown

          If you’ve ever woken up at 11am unable to face the day. If you’ve ever stared at a screen for an hour without taking in a word. If you’ve ever felt like the volume on your own life got turned down, like you’re behind glass, watching yourself go through the motions... you’ve maybe been in some form of stuck dorsal.

          Shutdown.

          It’s perhaps the most misunderstood of the three stuck states and the one people get most ashamed of. It looks like laziness from the outside. It feels like nothing from the inside. It’s neither.

          What stuck shutdown looks like across the four columns

          Cognitions
          Slow, foggy, absent. Can’t think clearly. Decisions feel impossible. Everything feels pointless or hopeless. Reading the same sentence three times without absorbing it. Internal monologue: nothing matters. I don’t care. I’m useless. What’s the point.
          Emotions
          Flat, numb, empty. Not sad exactly. The dial got turned to zero. You might cry without feeling it. Want to feel something, anything, and can’t find the feeling.
          Sensations
          Heavy, cold, leaden. Limbs feel weighted. Body feels distant, like it belongs to someone else. Reduced appetite or eating without tasting. Sleep that doesn’t restore. Voice goes quiet or monotone. Difficulty with eye contact.
          Impulses
          Hide, sleep, disappear, scroll, retreat. The pull is away from people, away from tasks, away from your own life. Not because you don’t care. Because the part of you that cares went offline to protect itself.

          This is what depression looks like through a polyvagal lens. It’s what burnout looks like. It’s what trauma response looks like when fight and flight weren’t available or successful and so the system collapsed instead, which is what it evolved to do.

          Why your nervous system shuts down

          Dorsal vagal immobilization is the oldest survival response we have. Older than fight. Older than flight. When mobilization isn’t available, when fighting won’t work, when fleeing won’t work, when the threat is too big or too long or inside us, the system drops into immobilization as a survival strategy.

          A few common reasons people end up stuck in dorsal:

          Chronic overwhelm. Long enough exposure to stress with no recovery and the system stops trying to mobilize. It conserves.

          Inescapable situations. Childhood environments, abusive relationships, jobs you can’t leave. The system learns there’s no exit, so it stops looking for one.

          Repeated activation without resolution. Years of fight-or-flight that never got to discharge. Eventually the system flips the breaker into collapse.

          Grief, loss, illness. Real losses that the body needs to mourn through a slower, quieter state.

          Sometimes there isn’t a clear cause. Stuck dorsal doesn’t always trace back to a single thing. Sometimes the system has just been carrying too much for too long. And maybe one extra little thing happens that tips an overwhelmed system into shutdown.

          Shutdown isn’t a malfunction. It’s a useful and normal function; an unconscious temporary biological state. The fact that it doesn’t feel good doesn’t mean it’s wrong. That’s your conscious experience of your stuck dorsal state.

          What coming out of stuck dorsal shutdown actually looks like

          You cannot push out of shutdown. Trying to force yourself out usually makes it worse. Shame doesn’t move you. Discipline doesn’t move you. Cold plunges and breathwork hacks don’t move you, despite what the algorithm says.

          What does move you is ventral vagal safety, in small repeated doses, until the system has enough cumulative input to allow the dorsal influence to lessen and the sympathetic influence to increase.

          Use the Polyvagal Current model above to follow the sequence of state shifts. It starts in stuck dorsal: shutdown is dominant (blue), but safety (yellow) increases with the slider. When enough safety is present (~50% in the model), the shutdown mixes with safety and turns into stillness (green). From stillness, the body can continue to self-regulate out of shutdown and into sympathetic (red). However, in this model, the safety state welcomes the sympathetic activation, mixing with it to form play (orange). Self-regulation continues with more safety containing the system and eventually into stillness again.

          The above is an ideal form of coming out of stuck shutdown. But life is not that simple. In real life:

          • Stuck shutdown is resistant to change
          • Moments of mixing safety and shutdown come and go
          • Increased sympathetic activation is likely, showing up as irritability and aggression
          • As sympathetic returns, it’s likely that shutdown will resist, resulting in freeze

          It’s essential to build a strong foundation of ventral vagal safety. All the system’s regulation efforts are built on top of this.

          Coming out of stuck shutdown in practice

          Let’s look at how to come out of stuck shutdown through deliberate practice.

          Reduce sensory input. Shutdown doesn’t like sensory overload. Dim lighting. Silence. Smaller spaces. Comfort. Warmth.

          Small movement, not big movement. Shutdown prefers small. A short walk. Stretching. Wiggling your toes. The body has to be invited back, not yanked.

          Let some activation in. As you come out of shutdown, you’ll often pass through irritability, restlessness, even anxiety. That’s your sympathetic coming online. You’re close to play at this point. Don’t push back down. The activation is the path through. Continue to build safety and feel into sympathetic as you can.

          Settle into stillness, not back into shutdown. When you’ve been in shutdown a long time, anything that feels like “lying down quietly” can feel like a relapse. It isn’t necessarily. Stillness, dorsal with safety, feels warm, not cold. Present, not absent. The four columns tell you which one you’re in.

          Co-regulation. Borrow someone else’s nervous system. A safe person, a pet, a body next to yours. Co-regulation is faster than self-regulation when you’re in deep shutdown. If you don’t have a safe person, a familiar place or a piece of music your body knows can serve as an anchor.

          State two

          Stuck freeze

          Freeze is the most confusing of the three stuck states, usually.

          First, people struggle to recognize the difference between freeze and shutdown. Second, they struggle to see it alive within themselves.

          Shutdown is “off.” Fight-or-flight is “on.” Freeze is both, at the same time.

          You know freeze when you’ve lived it. Your heart is pounding but you can’t move. Your mind is racing but you can’t think clearly. You know you should do something but can’t start. Not because you don’t want to, of course. Quite the opposite. Because something inside has locked the controls.

          People call it deer in headlights. Procrastination. Brain fog. Paralysis. Indecision. The labels miss the mechanism. Freeze isn’t a single nervous system state. It’s a collision of two. Sympathetic activation underneath, dorsal immobilization on top. The accelerator and the parking brake at the same time.

          In the Polyvagal Current above, that’s two of the three circles firing into each other at once.

          Sympathetic + dorsal vagal = freeze

          What stuck freeze looks like across the four columns

          Cognitions
          Fast but aimless. Racing in a loop. Catastrophizing without resolution. I should. I need to. Why can’t I. What’s wrong with me. Thinking is spinning but with no traction. Sometimes the opposite: mind goes blank in a way that feels more like a wall than an emptiness.
          Emotions
          Anxious, panicky, ashamed, helpless, confused. Often a thick layer of self-judgment: what is wrong with me that I can’t just do this. The shame is louder than the original fear much of the time.
          Sensations
          Locked, tight, immobile, but with activation underneath. Muscles tense. Breath shallow or held in the chest. Sometimes trembling or buzzing under the skin. Sometimes the opposite, a heavy, weighted stillness. The hallmark is the combination high arousal without movement.
          Impulses
          The impulse to do something is there, but blocked. You want to run, but you can’t move. You want to speak, but your throat closes. You want to start the task, but your hands won’t pick up the pen. The intention is there. The action gate is shut.

          People stuck in freeze will have high levels of activation, followed by low levels of activation. Their body spirals in a freeze for much of the day, then collapses in shutdown the rest. This cycle plays out endlessly.

          Why your nervous system freezes

          Freeze happens when your nervous system mobilizes in sympathetic and also immobilizes, whether through force or perception. Dorsal vagal locks the sympathetic activation in place. The result is a system with a foot on the gas and the brake at the same time.

          A few common reasons people end up stuck in freeze:

          Conflicting drives. Part of you wants to act; part of you can’t. Mobile and immobile at the same time.

          History of unsuccessful action. Childhoods where speaking up made things worse, where fighting was punished, where running away wasn’t possible or where danger was always present yet unpredictable. The system learned: don’t move.

          Overload. Too many demands, too many options, too many people wanting different things. The system can’t pick a direction, so it picks none.

          Coming out of a stuck freeze is a delicate, slow process requiring a firm anchoring in your safety state.

          What coming out of stuck freeze actually looks like

          As I’m sure you know, you can’t think your way out of freeze. Thinking is one of the things freeze is locking. Trying to talk yourself out of freeze with logic is like trying to push a car forward with the parking brake on. The brake has to release first.

          Coming out of freeze necessarily requires the shutdown immobilization brake releasing. And to do that, the system needs a lot of safety activation.

          Safety thaws the freeze. Once thawed, the once-frozen flight/fight activation can release.

          Ideally, you recover from freeze slowly. The underlying sympathetic activation can be intense, driving you into desperate actions that go nowhere, like isolating and phone-binging, hours in the gym per day, or even self-harm.

          The system needs to withdraw the shutdown brake a little bit, then release the sympathetic energy a little bit. This process happens repeatedly.

          Use the Polyvagal Current slider above. It’s set to the stuck freeze position (purple). As you move the Safety Influence slider up, ventral vagal safety (yellow) grows. As it grows and reaches the midpoint, the freeze thaws, shutdown (blue) diminishes, and sympathetic (red) emerges. Continue to add safety with the slider, and sympathetic merges with safety into play (orange), then more into safety (yellow) and eventually into stillness (green).

          In real life, no, it’s not that clean. Decoupling shutdown and sympathetic takes time. And the system will reject the process as safety builds. There will likely be lots of friction, doubt, and layers of once-frozen pains will emerge.

          Again, safety is essential for this process.

          Coming out of stuck freeze in practice

          Here are some helpful tips for thawing a stuck freeze.

          Intentional, mindful movement. For someone in freeze, they may have moments of intense activation. I highly recommend movement with mindfulness. Running endlessly and spending hours in the gym only physically exhausts you. It does not result in actual freeze unstucking. Actually pay attention to the experience of movement. This helps the system to unstuck.

          Small moments of mindfulness. I don’t expect you to meditate for 30 minutes when you’re in a stuck freeze. Instead, spend thirty seconds mindfully connecting with the outside world while moving, like during a walk or during morning pushups. Slowly work your way toward stillness.

          Direct the energy somewhere useful. As you successfully thaw, the underlying flight/fight needs an outlet. Plan ahead of time what you want that to be, whether movement or creativity or productivity. Eventually, you’ll connect so deeply with the once-frozen, flight/fight that it will tell you what it needs. For now, listen as best you can, then give it a chosen, intentional outlet.

          Then settle. Stillness is on the far side of the activation, not before it. Trying to “calm down” before the activation has discharged will likely refreeze the system.

          Note what’s not in this list: insight, willpower, positive thinking, breathing exercises designed to make you “relax.” Freeze responds to small, mindful, intentional physical action much more reliably than to mental effort.

          State three

          Stuck sympathetic flight/fight

          Stuck fight-or-flight might have the most language and diagnostic terms dedicated to it: anxiety, anger, stress, always on, type A, driven... The labels make it sound like a personality. But it’s not.

          Fight-or-flight is your sympathetic nervous system mobilizing to act on a threat.

          • Acute mobilization is the appropriate response when an actual threat is present.
          • Chronic mobilization, when no threat is actually here but the system can’t stand down, is the stuck version. Your body is fighting a tiger that left the room three years ago.

          What stuck flight/fight looks like across the four columns

          Cognitions
          Racing, urgent, narrow. Thoughts come fast and fixate on threats: what could go wrong, who is judging you, what you forgot, what you have to do. Catastrophic loops. Worst-case scanning. The thinking feels productive (like problem-solving) but it usually isn’t generating solutions. It’s burning fuel endlessly.
          Emotions
          Anxious, irritated, angry, worried, urgent. Often a low background hum of dread or pressure even when nothing is wrong. Sudden flashes of anger over small things. Quick to startle. Easily defensive.
          Sensations
          Fast heart, shallow breath, tight chest, clenched jaw, buzzing under the skin. Difficulty being still. Difficulty falling asleep. A sense of being “on edge” without being able to point to what’s threatening.
          Impulses
          To act, to fix, to fight, to escape, to control, to talk fast, to do more, to leave. Fidgeting. The body wants to go. There’s nowhere to go. The energy stays in the system, building.

          People stuck in flight/fight can get a lot done if they have a means to channel their activation. That doesn’t result in the stuckness actually alleviating, unfortunately. So, they repeat a productivity pattern day after day. They may also have coping mechanisms. Eventually, these methods are not as effective and the system slips into a shutdown.

          Why your nervous system fights or flees

          Sympathetic mobilization is supposed to be acute. Threat appears → system mobilizes → action is taken → threat resolves → system settles. The trouble is when there’s no clean resolution.

          A couple common reasons people end up stuck in fight-or-flight:

          Chronic, low-grade threat that never resolves. A job that demands too much. A relationship with unpredictable conflict. Financial pressure. The threat isn’t acute enough to fight or flee from, but it’s persistent enough that the system stays revved.

          Environmental shaping. A childhood filled with unpredictability. Bouncing around from home to home. Tension in the family. A partner prone to high mobilization without end. Not enough to shutdown and not enough to freeze. But enough to shape the system toward mobilization and away from connection.

          The mechanism is the same in all cases: your nervous system reads the current moment as requiring mobilization, and keeps mobilizing. The mobilization isn’t the problem. The system not being able to complete and settle is the problem.

          What coming out of stuck flight/fight actually looks like

          Telling an activated nervous system to “just relax” is like telling a running engine to stop revving without taking your foot off the gas. The activation is there for a reason. It needs to move through, not be suppressed.

          Check out the Current model above. It starts in stuck sympathetic (red). As you add safety, the ventral circle (yellow) increases, eventually combining with sympathetic, resulting in play (orange). As you utilize activation through play, the stuck flight/fight moves through the system and releases, leaving more space for safety and even stillness (green).

          Stuck flight/fight necessitates enough safety to combine into play. But play is with another safe person. If alone, safety can still combine with flight/fight, but it will show up as motivation. Use motivation to create, produce, and move.

          Coming out of flight/fight in practice

          So how do we utilize sympathetic activation?

          Discharge the activation. Whatever your body wants to do, give it a small physical version. Pace. Walk fast. Shake out your hands. Push against a wall. Stomp. Make noise: sigh, growl, sing, hum. The sympathetic branch is mobilized energy with nowhere to go. Give it somewhere to go that doesn’t damage anything.

          Slow your movement down on the back end. Pay attention to your body’s cues. You may notice that once you’ve discharged some, your body is ready for some settling.

          Orient. Look around your space mindfully, allowing your eyes to take you where they want. Your ears, too. And your other senses. Let your attention widen to the greater world as your body settles.

          Co-regulate. If settled enough, connect with a safe other person or pet.

          Remain open to stillness. Over time, you will have more capacity for immobilization, but be okay with it. Stillness is the result of regulation, not the tool. Be open to it as it presents itself.

          Flight/fight doesn’t do well with slowing down, so let your body move. Connect with it through movement. Let yourself feel powerful... but don’t overdo it. Be mindful. Pay attention to your muscles as they expand and contract. Notice your breath shifting naturally.

          Be. Don’t force.

          The throughline

          The path is the same in all three stuck states: add safety

          Across all three stuck states, the pattern is the same. The autonomic state isn’t the problem. The lack of safety is the problem. Add safety, and the state sorts itself back into its regulated expression. This is the single most useful reframe in the whole Polyvagal Current model.

          You don’t have to climb fully back to ventral. You have to ask: where can I add safety right now? Sometimes that’s a person. Sometimes it’s a place. Sometimes it’s slowing your exhale, or taking a walk, or putting your hand on your chest, or making a phone call to someone you trust. None of these are hacks. They are small inputs to a system that has been undersupplied with safety.

          Your real-world Safety Influence slider moves on its own when safety comes in. You don’t have to drag it. Your job is to keep adding small, sustainable, repeated safety signals, and to be patient enough to let the system respond on its own timeline.

          Some practical implications:

          Stop trying to fix the state. Trying to “get out of dorsal” or “calm down from sympathetic” is fighting the state. Adding safety is working with it, especially if you can listen to the needs of your stuck state.

          Trust the current. You’re not supposed to live 100% in ventral. Your self-regulation current is supposed to flow into, out of, amongst, and between all of your primary and mixed states.

          Stuck is information. When you’re stuck, it means the safety in the system isn’t enough for the demand the system is facing. The solution might not be inside you. It might be that the demand needs to change.

          The same logic works for all three. The specifics differ, sure. Shutdown needs quiet, while sympathetic needs space, and freeze needs careful attention paid to potential overwhelm. But the underlying principle is identical: small, repeated, sustainable safety inputs, applied in the way your specific stuck state can accept them.

          The Current doesn’t promise you a permanent good state. It teaches you to read where you are and add what’s missing. And it shows you the benefit of slowly adding safety into your system.

          Over time

          A daily practice of unstucking

          I don’t believe in quick nervous system fixes or hacks or shortcuts. I believe in practice. Small, realistic, and sustainable practice tailored to your specific state.

          Unstucking isn’t a one-time event. It’s a repeated re-entry into yourself and the present moment.

          What helps over time:

          A daily anchor. One small thing you do every day that signals safety. A morning walk. Coffee on the porch. Five minutes of stillness before sleep. Not a productivity habit. A safety habit. Best if done mindfully.

          A safe relationship, even one. Co-regulation is nervous system medicine. If you don’t have a person, then a therapist, a community, or a pet.

          Permission to be in the regulated states. You’re allowed to be in play, stillness, motivation, intimacy, and safety. These are restorative and fulfilling.

          Tracking the four columns. Name the shift when you notice it. Or, when reflecting back on it. Naming reinforces the state and the awareness of the experience. Most people only name what’s wrong; learning to name what’s coming back online is its own practice.

          Honest assessment of your demands. Stuckness makes sense when put into life context. Your nervous system isn’t wrong. Yes, there is benefit to increasing your system’s capacity, but maybe you also need to reduce the demand on your system.

          Patience with friction. As you work on your stuckness, friction is going to happen. Your body wants to shift state, but the system as a whole may resist as it tries. Use compassion here.

          A caution

          When to get help

          The three stuck states overlap with real clinical territory:

          Chronic stuck dorsal overlaps significantly with clinical depression. If you’re having thoughts of harming yourself, if your daily functioning has eroded, please reach out to a therapist or your doctor.

          Chronic stuck freeze shows up as cycles of intensity and collapse. It’s also likely connected to acute traumatic incidents. Reach out to someone who specializes in trauma.

          Chronic stuck fight-or-flight overlaps with anxiety disorders, anger, and stress-related medical issues. A therapist can help. A primary care doctor is also worth seeing, since chronic sympathetic activation has real physical consequences and there are sometimes medical contributors that look identical to anxiety (thyroid, cardiac, hormonal).

          This page is education, not treatment. The Polyvagal Current is a map. A therapist is a guide. Both are useful, and they aren’t substitutes for each other.

          If you’re in crisis in the US, you can dial or text 988 to reach the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline.

          For helpers

          For clinicians and other helpers

          If you’re a therapist, coach, or other professional helper, here’s what this framework offers:

          A unified map of stuckness. Rather than treating depression, anxiety, and PTSD as separate clinical pictures, they (and more) are seen as patterns of the same underlying mechanism (insufficient safety in the system). For treatment-resistant clients, keep this in mind.

          Four-column observation. Clients eventually learn to track themselves through sensations and impulses, not just cognitions and emotions. This might be a challenge for clients who think more objectively, but progress can be made toward the inner world.

          A non-pathologizing frame. “Stuck” is more workable than “disordered.” Clients arrive with significant shame attached to their diagnostic labels. The Polyvagal Current and the stuck-state framework give them a vocabulary that’s accurate but not pathologizing. Hope underlies this thinking.

          A consistent path-out logic. All three stuck states share the same underlying intervention principle (add safety; let the system re-regulate). The specific practices differ by state, but the logic is unified. This is easier for clients and providers to internalize than numerous separate symptom-management protocols.

          For the model itself (the Polyvagal Current, the Safety Influence slider, and the three circles), see The Polyvagal Current. For the daily literacy practice that uses the model on yourself, see How to read your own nervous system.

          The page itself is freely linkable. Attribution to this page is appreciated.

          Quick answers

          FAQ

          Are these the only three stuck states?

          Yes. There are flavors within each, as all primary states are active to some degree all the time. But stuckness shows up as sympathetic, shutdown, or freeze. Clinical presentations and behavioral adaptations sort into one of the three or a recognizable blend.

          What about fawn and appeasement?

          Polyvagal Theory posits fawn as a mix of sympathetic and dorsal, which is freeze. I think of it as a behavioral adaptation to significant shutdown. Appeasement is suggested to be all three states active at the same time. I think of it also as a behavioral adaptation to significant shutdown. Watch my podcast episode to learn more.

          Can I be in more than one stuck state at once?

          Freeze is already a blend (sympathetic and dorsal at the same time). Beyond that, you can rapid-cycle between states: fight-or-flight that crashes into shutdown, shutdown that pulses back into freeze. The four-column observation will tell you which one is dominant in any given moment.

          Is stuck dorsal the same as depression?

          Polyvagal Theory suggests that a stuck, dominant dorsal vagal state is the biological explanation for depression. Depression is the clinical diagnosis.

          Does flight present different than fight when stuck?

          Flight shows up as anxiety, worry, and nervousness. Fight shows up as irritability, anger, and aggression.

          Can I get unstuck without therapy?

          Yes, generally, with daily practice, co-regulation in healthy relationships, and time. For chronic or trauma-related stuckness, therapy speeds and deepens the process and may be necessary. There’s no shame in either path.

          Will I ever stop getting stuck?

          The pattern softens with practice. You can live with much more emotional freedom and choice. More connection to self, environment, and others.
